description: Biohacking Village showcases emerging biotechnology research, security implications of medical devices and healthcare systems, and the DIY biology movement. The 25 talks cover medical device vulnerabilities, genetic engineering, sensory augmentation, biohacking ethics, and the future of personalized medicine and biology as a technology platform.

talks.title: Medical Device Ethics
talks.teaser: Ethical implications of implanted medical devices as evidence in legal cases and vulnerabilities discovered in contemporary healthcare technology.
talks.summary:
Ethics and Implications of Medical Technology

Implanted medical devices are keeping people alive, yet the same devices can become evidence in legal proceedings. This dual nature raises serious ethical questions about patient privacy and rights.

Vulnerability Discovery in Practice

The speakers discuss vulnerabilities discovered during security testing of medical devices, including pacemakers, neurostimulators, and drug delivery systems. These real-world examples demonstrate the risks that patients face when their life-sustaining devices lack proper security controls.

Modern Technological Advances

Neuroscience tools are now used by marketing firms and other commercial entities. The convergence of medical technology with broader surveillance and data collection represents a fundamental shift in privacy implications for medical device users.

Security and Patient Rights

The discussion emphasizes how medical device security impacts patient autonomy and legal protections, connecting device vulnerabilities to broader issues of bodily autonomy and informed consent.

talks.title: Psychoactive Chemicals in Combat
talks.teaser: Military research on psychoactive chemicals and enhancement protocols offers a foundation for grassroots biohackers and body augmenters pursuing their own experiments.
talks.summary:
Military Research in Psychoactive Chemistry

Key experiments and trials conducted by military branches reveal which chemical protocols work and which fail on human subjects. This research spans biological enhancement and chemical deterrents.

Implications for Biohackers

The speakers present this military research as a resource for grassroot scientists and body augmenters. While military science was developed in institutional settings with specific objectives, the underlying methodologies and findings are available for independent researchers to learn from.

From Enhancement to Deterrence

The range of research covers both performance enhancement (cognitive, physical, endurance) and defensive applications (deterrents, protective compounds). Understanding both allows biohackers to design safer experiments.

talks.title: Standardizing Deployment of Medical Devices
talks.teaser: Healthcare security vulnerabilities in unpatched medical device control systems and strategies for defending critical patient-care infrastructure.
talks.summary:
Healthcare Security Landscape

Healthcare organizations face escalating ransomware and breach attacks, with adversaries now targeting medical devices directly rather than only EHR and PACS systems. Older but functional medical device control systems often contain hundreds of unpatched vulnerabilities.

Aging Medical Infrastructure

Computerized medical supply cabinets and other devices installed years ago to improve efficiency now represent significant security liabilities. These systems lack modern security updates and controls, creating attack vectors that sophisticated malware like Medjack can exploit.

Direct Impact on Patient Safety

Medical device compromise poses existential risks beyond data breaches: infusion pump dosages can be altered, pacemaker programming can be manipulated, and surgical robots can be disabled. The speaker covers real scenarios where device compromise directly threatens patient life.

Defense and Standardization

The talk emphasizes strategies for deploying medical devices securely, including network segmentation, access controls, and establishing secure baseline configurations across healthcare organizations.

talks.title: Tales of a Healthcare Hacker
talks.teaser: Real-world hacking and social engineering attacks against healthcare networks and the security implications of electronic medical records and networked medical devices.
talks.summary:
The Healthcare Security Problem

Over the past decade, electronic medical records (EMRs) and networked medical devices have become healthcare infrastructure standards. Despite this critical role, vendors and consumers have neglected security implications of these systems.

Ethical Hacking in Healthcare

The speaker covers personal experiences conducting authorized penetration testing and social engineering attacks against healthcare networks. These real-world examples demonstrate how easily attackers can penetrate supposedly secure medical environments.

Common Security Issues

The talk highlights recurring security problems in healthcare networks: weak access controls, poorly segmented networks, lack of monitoring, and insufficient incident response procedures. Many of these issues are compounded by the legacy nature of much healthcare technology.

Real Life Stories

Through concrete examples, the speaker illustrates how security vulnerabilities in healthcare networks can be exploited and what defenders should prioritize when securing medical systems.

talks.title: Genomics and Personalized Medicine: Real Stories
talks.teaser: Personal stories of how genomic testing and personalized medicine can dramatically impact medical treatment and individual health outcomes.
talks.summary:
Genetic Testing and Medical Impact

Two speakers share contrasting personal stories about how genomic testing shaped their medical decisions and life trajectories. One story illustrates how genetic information literally saved a life through early intervention, while another shows tension between genetic knowledge and family dynamics.

Personalized Medicine Decisions

The speakers address practical questions: Should you get a genomic test? What can you learn from genetic testing? What are the risks? How do you choose a reliable test? The answers vary based on personal circumstances and values.

Data and Privacy Concerns

Genetic testing raises legitimate privacy concerns about data collection, retention, and potential misuse. The speakers discuss these issues alongside the medical benefits of personalized medicine.

Doctor-Patient Communication

Genetic information can put patients at odds with their physicians if doctors are unfamiliar with personalized medicine or skeptical of genetic testing. The talk explores how to navigate these conversations and advocate for patient autonomy.

talks.title: Hack Your Senses: Sensory Augmentation
talks.teaser: Technologies and implants that enable humans to sense beyond natural limits—magnetic fields, infrared light, wider color ranges—through devices like the BrainPort and emerging commercial biohacking products.
talks.summary:
Sensory Limits and Augmentation

Human senses operate within narrow frequency bands: eyes see specific colors, ears hear bounded frequency ranges, and we remain largely unaware of surrounding electromagnetic fields. Sensory augmentation extends perception beyond these natural limits.

Neuroscience of Perception

Dr. Paul Bach-y-Rita's 1960s research led to the BrainPort, a device that creates visual perception through an electrode grid on the tongue. This work demonstrated how the brain can learn to interpret novel sensory inputs through alternative pathways.

Commercial Biohacking Devices

Recent developments bring sensory augmentation outside medical settings. Examples include fingertip magnets, Neil Harbisson's auditory color perception system, and NeoSensory and Cyborg Nest products. These devices let users sense infrared light, electromagnetic fields, or other phenomena invisible to baseline human senses.

How Sensory Augmentation Works

The speaker explains the neurological mechanisms: how sensory information travels through nerves, how the brain interprets unfamiliar signals, and why a vibrating magnetic field sensor is fundamentally different from a compass even though both convey directional information.

talks.title: Hacking the Second Genetic Code
talks.teaser: Computational methods to decode the second genetic code—the rules governing which amino acids transfer RNAs carry—revealing variability that can be exploited in synthetic biology.
talks.summary:
The Genetic Code and Its Translation

The primary genetic code is well understood: triplets of nucleotides (codons) are recognized by transfer RNAs that carry corresponding amino acids, which the ribosome incorporates into growing protein chains. This process is the foundation of all life.

The Second Genetic Code

Less explored is the "second genetic code"—the rules determining which amino acid a transfer RNA carries. Unlike the primary genetic code which is relatively static across organisms, the second genetic code varies dramatically between species.

Computational Decryption

The speaker developed an information-theory-based computational method to elucidate the second genetic code from genomic sequences. This approach can extract the underlying rules from raw DNA data without requiring experimental determination.

Applications to Synthetic Biology

Understanding the second genetic code variability enables new possibilities in genetic engineering: creating custom synthetic organisms and designer organisms with modified translation mechanisms. This work supports emerging technologies in synthetic biology and genome editing.

talks.title: The Moral Imperative of Biohacking
talks.teaser: Ethical implications of the biohacker mindset, experimentation outside institutional safeguards, and governance frameworks to balance innovation with responsible biology.
talks.summary:
The Biohacking Ethics Problem

Rapidly evolving biotechnology advances have outpaced ethical and regulatory frameworks. Biohacking has potential consequences more serious than traditional technologies, making community discussion and ethical frameworks critical.

Ethical Questions in Practice

The hacker mindset brings both innovation and risk: the ability to experiment outside traditional research settings with their safety protocols, access to methodologies developed by non-benign parties, unforeseen consequences of new discoveries, and questions about who benefits from biotechnology.

Experimentation Without Institutional Safeguards

DIY and community biology labs operate with different constraints than academic or pharmaceutical research institutions. This freedom enables rapid innovation but also raises safety concerns for experimenters and the broader community.

Building Equitable Futures

The core ethical challenge: should we build biotechnology for billionaires or for the billions? This question underlies decisions about accessibility, regulation, and the purpose of biohacking as a movement.

talks.title: Total Recall: Implicit Learning as Cryptography
talks.teaser: Using implicit learning and human memory to create authentication that survives duress—encoding passwords into cognitive memory through serial interception sequence learning training.
talks.summary:
Memory and Authentication

Cognitive memory operates through three stages: encoding (converting information into memory), storage (maintaining memories), and retrieval (accessing stored information). Understanding these mechanisms enables novel authentication approaches.

Authentication Beyond Traditional Passwords

Standard password-based authentication has a critical flaw: under duress or torture, users can be coerced to reveal credentials. The talk explores authentication schemes that exploit memory limitations to create credentials users cannot consciously reveal.

Implicit Learning and SISL Training

Serial Interception Sequence Learning (SISL) training embeds passwords into implicit memory through repeated exposure and pattern recognition, distinct from explicit memorization. Implicitly learned sequences are harder to consciously access or articulate.

Forensic Hypnosis and Memory Recovery

The research considers whether forensic hypnosis could extract implicitly learned passwords. The speaker reviews current research on memory recovery and the practical security implications of this emerging authentication paradigm.

talks.title: Trigraph: Ethereum-based Teleradiology
talks.teaser: Decentralized Ethereum-based platform for secure teleradiology that eliminates intermediaries, reduces costs, and enables direct peer-to-peer collaboration between radiologists and patients globally.
talks.summary:
Teleradiology Industry and Problems

Teleradiology is an $8 billion annual industry enabling remote medical image interpretation. As healthcare increasingly emphasizes real-time medical imagery analysis for emergency situations, the systems enabling medical collaboration must be secure and reliable.

Blockchain-Based Infrastructure

Trigraph is an Ethereum-based application enabling anyone needing medical image interpretation to connect with radiologists anywhere in the world securely, privately, and without third-party intermediaries.

Privacy and Security Benefits

Blockchain infrastructure allows direct doctor-patient interaction while maintaining privacy through cryptographic protocols. Medical records remain under patient control rather than held by centralized healthcare corporations or teleradiology platforms.

Cost Reduction and Access

By eliminating intermediary platforms and their profit margins, direct blockchain-enabled teleradiology reduces costs for both patients and radiologists while maintaining security and reliability standards necessary for critical medical decisions.

talks.title: The Patient as CEO
talks.teaser: Converging technologies including wearables, AI, 3D printing, and robotics enable patients to become informed decision-makers and leaders in their own healthcare.
talks.summary:
Technology Convergence in Healthcare

Accelerating technological advances—wearable sensors, point-of-care diagnostics, 3D printing, tissue engineering, artificial intelligence, robotics, and network connectivity—fundamentally transform healthcare delivery and patient agency.

Patient Empowerment and Engagement

These technologies enable patients to move from passive recipients of care to active leaders in their healthcare teams. Wearables provide continuous health monitoring, point-of-care diagnostics enable immediate test results, and AI can provide personalized treatment recommendations.

Data and Crowd Intelligence

The convergence includes network effects and collective intelligence: patients contribute real-world data through wearables, share experiences through community platforms, and benefit from crowd-sourced medical knowledge and peer support.

Patient Control of Health

The speaker emphasizes how these advances place control of healthcare decisions back in patients' hands. Rather than relying solely on physician expertise, patients armed with personal health data and AI insights can make informed decisions about their own medical treatment and wellness strategies.

talks.title: Hacking the Internet of Dongs
talks.teaser: Security and privacy vulnerabilities in internet-connected adult toys and efforts to bring information security best practices to an under-researched branch of IoT.
talks.summary:
Internet of Dongs as IoT Security Research

Internet-connected sex toys represent an under-researched branch of IoT security. Like many IoT devices, these products suffer from security and privacy vulnerabilities that are more serious given their intimate and personal nature.

The Vulnerability Landscape

Commercial IoD devices have not typically received security auditing by the same researchers who focus on other IoT categories. This gap in research means vulnerabilities often go undiscovered and unpatched. Common issues include weak authentication, unencrypted data transmission, insecure cloud backends, and firmware vulnerabilities.

Privacy Implications

The intimate nature of these devices means privacy breaches carry uniquely serious consequences for users. Data collection practices, cloud storage of usage patterns, and potential for device compromise all pose privacy risks that exceed typical IoT privacy concerns.

Industry Engagement and Change

The Internet of Dongs project (internetofdon.gs) works to bring information security best practices to the adult toy industry through responsible disclosure, vendor education, and public awareness. The speaker covers the approach and progress in improving security standards across the industry.

talks.title: The Future is Fake Identities
talks.teaser: Tools for creating and managing multiple fake identities online and offline, enabling individuals to reclaim privacy and reduce exposure from digital tracking and surveillance.
talks.summary:
The Privacy Problem and Fake Identities

Digital and physical surveillance threats emanate from corporate data collection, government agencies, and malicious actors. Rather than relying on ineffectual regulations or incomprehensible privacy policies, individuals can take direct control through fake identities.

Fake Identities as Privacy Tools

Fake identities in the hands of individuals become a mechanism to swing the pendulum of privacy back to the people. These are not deceptive aliases for fraud, but rather legitimate proxies that individuals create, control, and manage for different contexts and purposes.

Real-World Usage Patterns

The company discussed in the talk has deployed tools enabling millions of fake identities across various applications: dating, shopping, selling, social media, political statements, and numerous other uses. Over 2 million active fake identities are in use and growing daily.

Buildable Privacy Infrastructure

The speakers share progress on tools that enable individuals to implement fake identities both offline and online. These systems support compartmentalization—maintaining separate identities for different contexts—enabling true privacy and agency.

talks.title: DIY Bioweapons and Regulation
talks.teaser: Capabilities for biological weapons production in community bio labs and regulatory approaches that balance maximum innovation freedom with effective monitoring and safety.
talks.summary:
Emerging Biotech Capabilities

Recent technological advances have dramatically reduced barriers to creating biological constructs, including engineered pathogens. What once required massive institutional resources can increasingly be accomplished in community or home bio labs with more affordable equipment.

DIY Biology and Dual-Use Technology

The same technologies enabling beneficial biohacking research—CRISPR gene editing, synthetic biology tools, DNA synthesis—can be misused to create dangerous organisms or biological weapons. This dual-use nature requires serious consideration.

Regulatory Challenges

Governments must balance innovation and freedom with biosecurity and public health protection. The speaker explores regulatory and legislative approaches that enable maximum innovation and accessibility while providing effective monitoring to prevent misuse.

Community Responsibility

The biohacking community itself plays a critical role in establishing norms, safety practices, and self-governance. The speaker emphasizes how grassroots safety culture and peer accountability are essential complements to formal regulation.

talks.title: Microscopes Are Stupid
talks.teaser: Low-cost IoT microscope accessory that transforms standard microscopes into digital whole-slide imaging devices, enabling distributed laboratory diagnosis and specimen analysis.
talks.summary:
The Diagnosis Problem

Conventional microscopes cannot autonomously diagnose disease—they are tools for observation requiring expert interpretation. What if microscopes themselves could diagnose? The Auto Diagnostic Assistant (ADA) project from NYU Tandon School of Engineering aims to enable this through digital imaging and machine learning.

ADA: Affordable Digital Microscopy

ADA is an extremely low-cost microscope accessory that turns a standard microscope into a digital imaging tool capable of creating whole-slide images (WSIs). It accomplishes the same tasks as expensive whole-slide imaging devices at a fraction of the cost, making it ideal for biohackers and resource-limited laboratories.

Connected Global Laboratory Network

The team's mission is to connect every laboratory in the world into a global network for specimen image sharing, study, and analysis. This distributed approach enables rapid consultation, collaborative research, and standardized diagnostic processes across geographic boundaries.

Technical Implementation

The team comprises hardware engineers, software developers, and machine learning specialists. They have validated accuracy through preclinical studies and presented research at the United States and Canadian Anatomical Pathology Conference (USCAP).

talks.title: The Brave New World of Bio Entrepreneurship
talks.teaser: Accessible pathways to biotech entrepreneurship through reduced research costs, automation, and software-driven efficiencies enabling founders at any background to build biology-based companies.
talks.summary:
The Democratization of Biotech

Historically, biotech companies required prestigious academic affiliations and millions in investment funding. Today, the convergence of cheaper research equipment, robotics, software, and production efficiency means anyone with insight can start a biotech company for a fraction of traditional costs.

IndieBio and Accelerated Innovation

IndieBio, the world's largest biotech accelerator, has funded and supported 70+ companies in under three years. The accelerator trains graduate students and first-time founders (without PhDs) to become successful entrepreneurs and has expanded biotechnology beyond traditional therapeutics and medical devices.

Diverse Application Domains

Biotech companies now operate across diverse sectors: food production, regenerative medicine, consumer products, neurotech, and bio-IT interfacing. This expansion demonstrates that biology is emerging as a fundamental technology platform like semiconductors or the internet.

Problem-Focused Innovation

IndieBio companies are solving major problems with biology as the technological foundation. The speakers highlight how democratized biotech tools enable novel solutions to problems previously constrained by cost and institutional access.

talks.title: Medical Industry Disruption: Blockchain
talks.teaser: Distributed ledger technologies and blockchain will fundamentally restructure global healthcare delivery, moving trust from centralized intermediaries to open protocols and enabling patient empowerment.
talks.summary:
Blockchain's Healthcare Potential

Over the next decade, blockchain and distributed ledger technologies will fundamentally change how healthcare is delivered worldwide. These technologies move trust from centralized controlling intermediaries to open-source protocols, freeing data and assets from traditional corporate interests.

Decentralization and Control

The blockchain provides a technical framework where verification and trust emerge from the protocol itself rather than from institutions. This shift enables patients, providers, and communities to interact directly without intermediaries taking cuts and controlling data.

Reconstructing Broken Systems

The current healthcare system has structural problems: misaligned incentives, restricted data flow, high costs from intermediary markups, and inadequate patient agency. Blockchain-based global health initiatives offer an opportunity to reconstruct these systems in fundamentally different ways.

Sustainable Wellness and Health Environments

The speaker emphasizes the possibility of reshaping healthcare around sustainable wellness and environments of health, supported by blockchain infrastructure that prioritizes individual and community wellbeing over corporate profit extraction.

talks.title: Biohackers Die
talks.teaser: Safety precautions and procedures in the biohacking community to minimize risk as experimental procedures become increasingly invasive and the movement matures.
talks.summary:
The Rising Risk Profile

Over the past decade, methods for pursuing human improvement have become increasingly invasive: internal implants, genetic modifications, neurochemical enhancements, and surgical augmentations carry higher stakes than earlier biohacking experiments.

Inevitability of Incidents

The biohacking community has been fortunate so far, but a death due to biohacking is likely if not inevitable as the movement expands and practitioners tackle more ambitious projects. This reality demands serious discussion of risk management and safety culture.

Precautions and Safety Practices

The speaker discusses precautions being implemented by biohackers to make procedures and projects as safe as possible. Topics include medical training, infection control, reversibility considerations, incremental testing, and peer review of experimental designs.

Community Safety Culture

Establishing strong safety norms within the biohacking community is essential—many practitioners work outside institutional oversight and cannot rely on institutional safety protocols. Self-governance and peer accountability become primary mechanisms for risk mitigation.

talks.title: The Scientific Method in Security Research
talks.teaser: Applying rigorous scientific methodology to security research increases credibility, produces more defensible findings, and strengthens the field of information security.
talks.summary:
The Research Problem in Security

Security research is frequently criticized for lacking process and adherence to traditional research methods. Much so-called research consists of tearing apart systems and exposing vulnerabilities—useful but lacking scientific rigor.

Scientific Method in Practice

The speaker demonstrates how rigorous scientific methodology can be applied to security research through his own work on insulin pump security, which led to widely-cited 2011 findings about medical device vulnerabilities.

Structured Hypothesis and Testing

Applying the scientific method means forming testable hypotheses, designing controlled experiments, documenting methodology, and drawing conclusions supported by evidence. This approach produces research that is reproducible and defensible.

Increasing Credibility and Impact

Security researchers who follow scientific methodology gain credibility with academic institutions, journalists, policymakers, and the media. The speaker argues that relatively small changes to how security research is conducted can bring greater outside credibility to important security work.

talks.title: Neurogenic Peptides: Smart Drugs and Cognitive Enhancement
talks.teaser: Structural and chemical changes to the brain and central nervous system through neurogenic peptides for cognitive enhancement, surpassing traditional neurotransmitter-based nootropics.
talks.summary:
The Challenge of Brain Plasticity

The adult brain has been understood as largely fixed: while the body continuously regenerates most cell types, new nerve cells in adult brains occur only in limited regions. The conventional wisdom suggested that "what you are born with is what you have to work with."

Structural Brain Changes

Recent research suggests this pessimistic view is wrong. Neurogenic peptides can induce productive structural changes to brain and central nervous system tissue, moving beyond traditional nootropics that operate primarily at the chemical (neurotransmitter) level.

Beyond Conventional Limits

Historically impossible milestones—lossless electrical conductivity, supersonic flight, running a four-minute mile—eventually became not just possible but standard benchmarks. The speaker argues that cognitive enhancement through reliable structural brain changes represents the next barrier to break.

Peptide-Based Enhancement

Neurogenic peptides appear to facilitate neuroplasticity and cellular growth in the brain, enabling more substantial cognitive improvements than traditional pharmaceutical approaches. The speaker discusses mechanisms and evidence for how peptides can produce lasting cognitive enhancement.

talks.title: Biotechnology Needs a Security Patch
talks.teaser: Security vulnerabilities in biotechnology infrastructure and the bio-economy, presented as theatrical song and interpretive dance exploring critical questions about biotech security.
talks.summary:
### The Paradigm Shift: From Attribution to Prevention
At 00:00 and 01:31, Supervisory Special Agent Edward You of the FBI's Weapons of Mass Destruction Directorate reflects on how the 2001 Anthrax mailings fundamentally altered federal law enforcement. Rather than investigating biological incidents solely after catastrophic harm occurs, the FBI shifted toward proactive outreach, intelligence sharing, and building partnerships with the biological and scientific communities to identify biosecurity risks early.

### Synthetic Biology and the Dual-Use Dilemma
At 04:31, You explains why the Director of National Intelligence categorized genome-editing tools like CRISPR as potential weapons of mass destruction. Synthetic biology enables desktop DNA synthesis and the digitization of biological functions. However, while molecular tools accelerate therapeutic discoveries, they simultaneously lower the barrier for rogue actors to synthesize virulent pathogens or weaponize benign microbes without traditional state-sponsored laboratory infrastructure.

### Big Data, Cloud Genomics, and the Bio-Economy
At 07:31 and 10:34, the presentation explores the convergence of biotechnology and cyber infrastructure. Millions of human genomic profiles are uploaded to consumer genealogical services, university repositories, and commercial cloud storage providers. You highlights how international biomanufacturing partnerships and foreign-subsidized gene sequencing facilities (such as BGI) create massive repositories of genetic data beyond domestic regulatory protections.

### Converging Breaches: Correlating Health and Identity Records
At 12:04 and 15:04, You analyzes the systemic threat posed by correlating massive cyber breaches—such as the Anthem health insurance and Office of Personnel Management (OPM) hacks—with genomic datasets. When biometric and health histories are linked with cryptographic genetic markers, adversaries gain the capability to target specific individuals, public officials, or demographic segments with precision biological agents, economic sabotage, or bespoke synthetic toxins.

### Patching the Bio-Economy Through Cybersecurity
Concluding from 19:34 to 24:05, You calls upon the DEF CON community to help "patch" the emerging bio-economy. He argues that the life sciences sector severely lacks cybersecurity hygiene, supply chain verification, and intrusion detection frameworks. Securing DNA sequencers, automated synthesis pipelines, and genetic intellectual property requires applying battle-tested cyber defense methodologies directly to biotechnology.

talks.title: Implantable Technology Show and Tell
talks.teaser: Introduction to implantable technology through market overview, hands-on demonstrations, and personal stories from practitioners of human augmentation.
talks.summary:
Implantable Technology Landscape

The speakers introduce implantable technology that is currently available on the market. Products range from simple passive implants to complex active devices with sensing and communication capabilities. Understanding the current landscape helps biohackers evaluate options and understand possibilities.

Market Overview

The speakers cover where implantable technology can be sourced, the range of products available, and the costs associated with different augmentation approaches. This practical information helps aspiring biohackers understand feasibility.

Hands-On Experience

The show-and-tell format enables audience members to see and handle actual implants and augmentation devices, creating direct engagement with technology that biohackers use to modify their bodies.

Personal Stories of Augmentation

The speakers share their own experiences becoming "augmentives" (people with bodily augmentations). These personal narratives illustrate what it's like to live with implants, the social dimensions of being visibly augmented, and the motivations driving people to modify themselves.
